title: 22. Interview: Write Through Cache
summary: Interview Q&A for Write Through Cache — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Write Through Cache interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the write-through cache pattern, and how does it differ from cache-aside?
**Answer:** Write-through is a caching pattern where every write goes to the cache and the cache synchronously writes through to the database before returning success — guaranteeing cache-DB consistency. The application calls `cache.put(key, value)`, the cache sets its in-memory entry, then synchronously calls the DB writer, and only returns success when both have completed. In cache-aside, the application writes to the DB and invalidates the cache, leaving a window where the cache may serve stale data until the next read re-fetches. Write-through eliminates that window — the cache is always a faithful reflection of the DB. The trade-off: write-through has higher write latency (waits for both writes) but reads are always fast and always fresh. Real-world: Amazon DynamoDB DAX supports write-through — `PutItem` writes to DAX's cache and DynamoDB synchronously, so reads from DAX always reflect the latest write.
**Visual:**
```
Cache-aside write:              Write-through write:
DB UPDATE -> cache DEL          cache SET -> DB UPDATE (synchronous)
   |                                |
   v                                v
next read misses, fetches       next read hits cache (always fresh)
stale data possible             no staleness window
write latency = DB only         write latency = cache + DB
```

### Q2. Why is write-through "always consistent"? What does that mean precisely?
**Answer:** Write-through is "always consistent" in the sense that the cache and the DB hold the same value for any key, at all times, from the perspective of any reader. Specifically: (1) After a successful write, both the cache and the DB have the new value — a subsequent read from the cache returns the new value. (2) During a write, the cache may transiently hold the new value while the DB write is in flight, but no read can complete until the write completes (the lock serializes them). (3) If the DB write fails, the cache write is rolled back, so neither has the new value — the cache reverts to the old value (or empties). (4) There is no window where the cache has the old value and the DB has the new value (which is the staleness window in cache-aside). This is consistency in the **linearizability** sense for a single key: all operations appear to occur in a single sequential order, and reads return the latest write. Note: this is per-key, per-shard consistency; cross-shard and cross-region consistency still require additional mechanisms.
**Visual:**
```
After successful write: cache == DB == new_value (consistent)
During write:           cache = new, DB = writing (locked, no reads)
On DB failure:          cache rolled back, DB unchanged (consistent, old value)

Contrast cache-aside:
After write:            DB = new, cache = DEL (next read misses)
Brief window:           DB = new, cache = old (if read raced with DEL)
```

### Q3. What is the write-latency overhead of write-through, and when is it acceptable?
**Answer:** Write-through latency = cache_write_time + DB_write_time, vs cache-aside latency = DB_write_time only (the cache DEL is fire-and-forget). For typical numbers: Redis write 0.5 ms + Postgres write 5 ms = 5.5 ms write-through vs 5 ms cache-aside — a 10% overhead. The overhead is acceptable when: (1) Write QPS is modest (the absolute added latency per write is small in aggregate). (2) Reads vastly outnumber writes — the read latency savings (always fast, always fresh) outweigh the write overhead. (3) The application requires read-your-writes consistency (a user must see their own write immediately) — without write-through, you'd need read-after-write to the DB, which is slower. (4) The DB is fast (e.g., DynamoDB single-digit ms) so the cache write is a small fraction. The overhead is unacceptable when: write QPS is very high (millions/sec), the DB is slow (100 ms writes), or the application tolerates eventual consistency. In those cases, write-behind (async) is better. Real-world: Amazon DAX write-through adds ~1 ms overhead to DynamoDB writes — acceptable for most apps, unacceptable for ultra-high-throughput counters.
**Visual:**
```
Write-through latency:    cache(0.5ms) + DB(5ms) = 5.5ms
Cache-aside latency:      DB(5ms) + cache_DEL(0.5ms async) = 5ms
Overhead: 0.5ms (10%)

Acceptable when:           Unacceptable when:
- reads >> writes           - writes >> reads
- read-your-writes needed   - DB writes are slow (100ms+)
- DB is fast                - write QPS is millions/sec
```

### Q4. What is cache pollution in write-through, and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** Cache pollution occurs because write-through populates the cache with **every written key**, even keys that are never subsequently read. If a workload writes to a long tail of cold keys (e.g., logging events, telemetry, one-time updates), the cache fills with entries that are never accessed, causing LRU to evict actually-hot keys and degrading hit rate for the keys that matter. Mitigations: (1) **Don't cache write-only keys** — the application marks certain write paths as "write-through but don't populate" (write to DB only, skip the cache set); reads of these keys go to the DB. (2) **Short TTL on write-through entries** — set a short TTL (e.g., 60 seconds) so polluted entries evict quickly if not read. (3) **Separate caches for read-heavy vs write-heavy data** — read-heavy data uses write-through; write-heavy data uses write-behind or no cache. (4) **LRU with admission control** — only promote a key to the cache after N accesses (TinyLFU, W-TinyLFU), so one-time writes don't pollute. (5) **Segmented cache** — keep a small "recently written" segment and a larger "frequently read" segment; promote from one to the other based on access count. Real-world: Caffeine (Java cache) uses W-TinyLFU admission control precisely to defeat cache pollution from one-time writes.
**Visual:**
```
Without mitigation:
  writes to 1M cold keys -> cache fills with cold entries
                          -> hot keys evicted -> hit rate drops

With W-TinyLFU admission:
  write to cold key -> DB only (not cached)
  read cold key 2nd time -> promote to cache
  hot keys stay in cache, cold keys don't pollute
```

### Q5. How does write-through compare to write-behind (write-back), and when do you choose each?
**Answer:** Write-through: write to cache + DB synchronously; consistent but slow. Write-behind (write-back): write to cache only, asynchronously flush to DB later (batched); fast but inconsistent and loss-prone if the cache crashes before flushing. Choose write-through when: correctness is critical (financial transactions, inventory, auth), reads must reflect writes immediately, the DB can handle the write QPS, and write latency is acceptable. Choose write-behind when: write QPS exceeds DB capacity (must batch), data loss is tolerable (view counts, telemetry, like counts), eventual consistency is acceptable, and the application can tolerate a window where the cache has data the DB doesn't. Real-world: Amazon DAX defaults to write-through (correctness); Redis used for view counters at YouTube/Reddit is often write-behind (batch flush every second, accept small loss on crash). The hybrid pattern is "write-through for critical fields, write-behind for analytics fields" within the same application — e.g., a shopping cart's items are write-through (must be correct), but the "last viewed" timestamp is write-behind (loss-tolerant).
**Visual:**
```
Write-through:        Write-behind:
cache + DB (sync)     cache only (async flush to DB)
latency: high         latency: low
consistency: strong   consistency: eventual
loss on crash: none   loss on crash: unflushed writes

Choose:
- correctness-critical -> write-through
- high-throughput, loss-tolerant -> write-behind
```

### Q6. What happens if the DB is down in a write-through system?
**Answer:** If the DB is down, every write-through `put` fails (the DB write step errors). The cache rolls back its in-memory write (reverts to old value or deletes the entry) and returns an error to the application. The application cannot write — it must either fail the user request or queue the write for retry. Reads may still succeed if the keys are already in the cache (the cache hasn't lost data just because the DB is down), but reads of uncached keys will fail too (the DB is down). Mitigations: (1) **Queue writes for retry** — if the DB is down, enqueue the write in a durable queue (Kafka, SQS) and replay when the DB recovers; the cache serves reads from its current state. (2) **Fall back to cache-aside mode** — temporarily disable write-through and accept cache-aside semantics (write to DB when it recovers, invalidate cache); reads may serve stale data but writes don't fail. (3) **Multi-AZ DB** — failover to a standby DB so writes continue. (4) **Circuit breaker** — stop attempting DB writes for a cooldown period to avoid hammering a recovering DB. (5) **Accept the failure** — for some apps, failing writes during DB outage is correct (better to reject than to write inconsistent data). Real-world: DynamoDB DAX fails writes when DynamoDB is unavailable — applications must retry or failover.
**Visual:**
```
DB down:
  put(key, val) -> cache SET -> DB write FAILS -> rollback cache -> return error
  get(key)      -> if cached, return (works); if not cached, DB read fails -> error

Mitigations:
  + queue writes for retry (Kafka)
  + multi-AZ DB failover
  + circuit breaker (stop hammering DB)
  + accept failure (correctness over availability)
```

### Q7. Does write-through eliminate all consistency issues? What are its limits?
**Answer:** No — write-through provides **per-key linearizability** within a single cache instance or shard, but it does not solve all consistency issues: (1) **Cross-shard consistency** — if the cache is sharded (Redis Cluster), a write to shard A and a read from shard B may see different values until replication catches up; write-through is consistent within a shard, but cross-shard consistency requires quorum or synchronous cross-shard replication. (2) **Cross-region consistency** — write-through in region A doesn't make the cache in region B fresh until cross-region replication propagates; region B's cache may serve stale data. (3) **Multi-key transactions** — write-through doesn't provide atomicity across multiple keys; if you write key1 and key2, a concurrent reader may see key1=new but key2=old. Use a transactional cache (e.g., Redis MULTI/EXEC) or a database transaction. (4) **Cache failure between write and ack** — if the cache crashes after the DB write but before returning success, the application retries, potentially double-writing; idempotency keys mitigate. (5) **Read-your-writes across services** — if service A writes via write-through and service B reads from a different cache, B may not see A's write until cross-cache invalidation. For true global consistency, you need a globally-replicated cache with synchronous replication or a single-region write path with cross-region invalidation.
**Visual:**
```
Write-through provides:
  per-key, per-shard linearizability (cache == DB)

Does NOT provide:
  cross-shard consistency    (need quorum / sync replication)
  cross-region consistency   (need global sync replication)
  multi-key atomicity        (need transactions)
  cross-service consistency  (need shared cache or invalidation)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Amazon DynamoDB DAX is a write-through cache. Your e-commerce application writes inventory updates and immediately re-displays the product page. Why is DAX write-through the right choice here?
**Answer:** The application displays the product page immediately after the inventory write, so the user must see their update reflected — this is **read-your-writes consistency**. With cache-aside (write to DB, invalidate cache), the next read would miss and re-fetch from DynamoDB, adding ~5 ms of latency and a brief window where the cache could serve stale data if invalidation raced with a concurrent read. With DAX write-through, the `PutItem` call updates both DAX's cache and DynamoDB synchronously, so the immediate subsequent `GetItem` from DAX returns the fresh value in sub-millisecond — no miss, no race, no stale data. The write-latency overhead (DynamoDB write + DAX cache write, ~6 ms vs ~5 ms) is negligible for inventory updates (low write QPS per product), and the read latency savings (sub-ms vs 5 ms) compound across the millions of reads per peak hour. For inventory specifically, correctness matters — overselling due to stale cache is a real business problem — so write-through's consistency guarantee is essential. Real-world: Amazon reports DAX reduces DynamoDB read latency by 10× while maintaining read-your-writes consistency for exactly this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
Inventory update -> display page:
  cache-aside: write DB, DEL cache, next read misses (5ms) -> re-display (stale risk)
  write-through: write DAX+DynamoDB, next read hits DAX (<1ms) -> immediate fresh
```

### Q2. Your banking application uses write-through for account balances. A user transfers $100 from account A to account B. The write to A succeeds but the write to B fails. What happens, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** This is the classic **multi-key atomicity** problem that write-through does not solve. The transfer is two writes (decrement A, increment B); if the second fails, the system is in an inconsistent state — A is debited but B is not credited, so $100 has disappeared. Write-through only guarantees per-key consistency, not multi-key atomicity. Fixes: (1) **Database transaction** — wrap both writes in a single DB transaction (`BEGIN; UPDATE A; UPDATE B; COMMIT;`); if either fails, the transaction rolls back and neither write persists. The cache must be updated only after the transaction commits (or use a write-through-with-transaction pattern that updates both cache entries atomically after the DB transaction). (2) **Saga pattern** — break the transfer into compensating transactions: debit A, credit B, and if credit B fails, compensate by re-crediting A. (3) **Event sourcing** — write a "transfer" event to an append-only log; a downstream processor applies the debits and credits atomically. (4) **Two-phase commit** — for cross-service transfers (A in service 1, B in service 2), use 2PC or a coordinator like Seata. For banking, option 1 (DB transaction) is standard — never use bare write-through for multi-key financial operations. Real-world: banks use ACID transactions for transfers; caches sit in front for reads, not for transfer atomicity.
**Visual:**
```
Transfer A -> B:
  cache.put(A, balance-100) -> DB UPDATE A (success)
  cache.put(B, balance+100) -> DB UPDATE B (FAILS)
  Result: A debited, B not credited -> $100 lost!

Fix: DB transaction
  BEGIN
  UPDATE A SET balance = balance - 100
  UPDATE B SET balance = balance + 100
  COMMIT (or ROLLBACK on failure)
  -> then update cache for both A and B
```

### Q3. You're caching user session data with write-through. A user logs out, and the session is deleted. How do you handle the delete in write-through?
**Answer:** Deletion in write-through is symmetric to write: the application calls `cache.delete(key)`, the cache deletes its in-memory entry, then synchronously deletes (or marks as expired) the DB entry, and returns success. After the delete, both the cache and DB agree the key is gone. Reads of a deleted key return "not found" — either from the cache (if negative-cached) or from the DB. Important considerations: (1) **Negative caching** — after the delete, cache "not found" for a short TTL (e.g., 60 seconds) so repeated reads of the deleted session don't hit the DB. (2) **Idempotency** — deleting a non-existent key should succeed (return success even if the key wasn't there), so retries after a network blip don't fail. (3) **Order** — delete from the DB first (so if the cache delete fails, the DB is correct and the next read misses and re-fetches... but the DB says "not found", so the cache will be updated to "not found"); or delete from the cache first (so concurrent reads miss and see "not found" from the DB). Convention varies; the key is to handle both orders consistently. (4) **Audit log** — for security-sensitive deletes (logout, account closure), log the delete event before performing it, so the audit trail survives even if the delete fails. Real-world: AWS DAX supports `DeleteItem` with write-through semantics for exactly this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
Logout -> delete session:
  cache.delete(session_id)
    -> delete from cache (in-memory)
    -> delete from DB (synchronous)
    -> return success
  next read: cache miss -> DB "not found" -> cache negative (60s TTL) -> return None
```

### Q4. Your write-through cache is showing high write latency (50 ms p99). The DB write alone is 5 ms. Where is the extra 45 ms coming from?
**Answer:** Write-through latency = cache_write + DB_write + overhead. If DB_write is 5 ms and total is 50 ms, the extra 45 ms is in cache_write or overhead. Likely causes: (1) **Cache lock contention** — if the cache uses a single global lock for writes (as in the simple implementation above), concurrent writes serialize on the lock, queueing up; with 100 concurrent writes, each waits for 99 others. Fix: per-key locks or sharded locks. (2) **Cache replication** — if the cache is replicated (Redis Cluster with synchronous replication to replicas), the write waits for replica acks; this can add tens of ms. Fix: use asynchronous replication, or accept the latency for consistency. (3) **Network latency to cache** — if the cache is in a different AZ or region, each write incurs cross-AZ latency (1–2 ms) or cross-region (30+ ms). Fix: co-locate cache and application in the same AZ. (4) **Cache write amplification** — if the write triggers additional cache updates (e.g., updating indexes, sorted sets, materialized views), each adds latency. (5) **Serialization** — if the value is large (e.g., a 1 MB blob), serialization + network transfer takes time. (6) **Cache client overhead** — connection pool waits, command queueing, retry storms. Diagnose by adding per-step timing: cache_write_ms, db_write_ms, total_ms; the gap reveals the culprit. Real-world: Redis Cluster synchronous replication is a common culprit — switch to asynchronous for write-through workloads.
**Visual:**
```
Write latency 50ms, DB write 5ms -> 45ms unaccounted:
  + cache lock contention?   (single global lock serializes writes)
  + cache replication?       (sync replica ack adds 10-30ms)
  + network latency?         (cross-AZ 1-2ms, cross-region 30ms)
  + serialization?           (large value, JSON encoding)
  + cache client overhead?   (pool waits, command queue)

Diagnose: per-step timing
  cache_write_ms | db_write_ms | total_ms
       45ms           5ms          50ms   -> cache is the bottleneck
```

### Q5. You're building a real-time leaderboard for a game. Player scores update frequently (millions of writes/sec) and reads are also frequent. Is write-through appropriate?
**Answer:** No — write-through is inappropriate for a high-write-QPS leaderboard. Reasons: (1) **Write QPS too high** — millions of writes/sec means the DB must handle that QPS synchronously, which is expensive (DynamoDB at 1M writes/sec costs ~$5M/year); write-through doesn't reduce DB write load. (2) **Per-write latency overhead** — adding 0.5–1 ms of cache write per DB write at millions/sec is a huge aggregate overhead. (3) **Cache pollution** — every player's score is written through, but only the top-N are ever read; the cache fills with millions of cold entries. (4) **Atomicity** — leaderboard updates need atomic increment-and-rank, which write-through doesn't provide. Better approaches: (a) **Redis sorted set (ZSET)** — `ZADD leaderboard score player` is atomic, in-memory, and supports `ZRANGE` for top-N; the DB is updated asynchronously (write-behind) for persistence. (b) **Write-behind batching** — batch score updates in memory, flush to DB every second; lose at most 1 second of updates on crash. (c) **Approximate leaderboard** — sample top players, recompute every minute; perfect consistency is not needed for a game leaderboard. Real-world: Discord, Reddit, and most game leaderboards use Redis ZSETs with write-behind to the persistent store; write-through is never used at this scale.
**Visual:**
```
Leaderboard at 1M writes/sec:
  write-through: 1M DB writes/sec -> $5M/year DynamoDB cost (unacceptable)
  + cache pollution (every player cached, only top-N read)

Better:
  Redis ZSET (atomic ZADD, in-memory) -> write-behind to DB every 1s
  -> DB sees 1 write/sec (batched), cache is the source of truth for reads
```

### Q6. Your multi-region application uses write-through in each region. A user in region A writes; a user in region B reads 100 ms later. Does B see A's write?
**Answer:** Not necessarily — write-through provides per-region consistency, not cross-region consistency. Region A's write-through updates region A's cache and region A's DB. For region B to see the write, two things must happen: (1) The DB write must replicate from region A to region B (typical cross-region replication lag is 100 ms – several seconds for asynchronous replication). (2) Region B's cache must be invalidated or updated — if region B has the old value cached, it will serve stale data until its TTL expires or it's explicitly invalidated. With 100 ms elapsed, region B's DB may have the new value (if replication is fast) but region B's cache likely still has the old value (no invalidation has reached it). Fixes: (1) **Cross-region cache invalidation** — when region A writes, publish an invalidation event to a global Pub/Sub (Kafka, Redis Pub/Sub); region B's cache subscribes and invalidates the key. (2) **Global cache** — use a single globally-replicated cache (e.g., Redis with synchronous cross-region replication) so all regions see the same cache; very expensive. (3) **Read-your-writes via session pinning** — after a user writes in region A, route their subsequent reads to region A for a few seconds (until replication catches up); other users may see stale data. (4) **Accept eventual consistency** — for many apps, a 1-second cross-region staleness is fine. Real-world: Netflix uses event-driven invalidation via Kafka to propagate cache invalidations across regions within seconds.
**Visual:**
```
Region A writes:
  cache A (updated) + DB A (updated) -> write-through consistent in A
  -> async replication to DB B (100ms-1s)
  -> cache B still has old value (no invalidation) -> STALE in B

Fix: cross-region invalidation
  A writes -> publish invalidate(key) to Kafka
            -> B subscribes -> cache B invalidates -> next read fetches fresh
```

### Q7. Your team migrates from cache-aside to write-through for user profiles. After migration, write QPS to the DB doubles. Why, and what do you do?
**Answer:** Write QPS to the DB doubling is surprising because write-through should write to the DB exactly once per application write (same as cache-aside). Likely causes: (1) **Retries due to cache-write failures** — if the cache write fails (network blip, Redis down), the application retries the entire `put`, causing a duplicate DB write; with cache-aside, the DB write succeeded and the cache DEL was fire-and-forget, so no retry. Fix: make the write idempotent (idempotency keys) or retry only the cache write, not the DB write. (2) **Application now writes through the cache for fields that previously didn't cache** — during migration, the team enabled write-through for more fields than were cached before, so previously uncached writes now go through the cache path; this is a behavior change, not a bug, but explains higher DB write QPS. (3) **The cache is calling the DB writer twice** — a bug in the wrapper (e.g., retry-on-timeout even on success) double-writes. (4) **Write amplification from cache indexes** — if the cache maintains indexes (e.g., a sorted set of users by last-active), each write updates the index, which may trigger additional DB writes. (5) **Loss of write coalescing** — cache-aside may have batched writes (multiple updates to the same key in quick succession coalesced into one DB write); write-through writes each one immediately, so the DB sees more writes. Diagnose by comparing per-key write counts before/after; if the same key is written twice as often, it's a retry/coalescing issue. Fix the specific cause; if it's loss of coalescing, consider write-behind for high-frequency updates.
**Visual:**
```
Before (cache-aside):
  app write -> DB (1 query) -> DEL cache (async)

After (write-through):
  app write -> cache SET -> DB (1 query) -> ack
  but: cache SET fails -> retry -> DB (2 queries)  <-- duplicate!
  or: 5 app writes/sec to same key -> 5 DB writes (no coalescing)

Fix:
  + idempotency keys (retries don't duplicate)
  + write-behind for high-frequency keys (batch / coalesce)
  + audit wrapper for double-write bugs
```
